May there never be any forgetfulness or loss. By the power of my vows and conduct, may a single rain of flowers produce sounds within this great assembly to bear witness to my oath, ensuring that the Dharma does not fail to benefit the multitudes;
should the flowers possess faults, let them bear fruit as such. Second, the sound possesses two functions:
it induces awakening and serves as a basis for study. For this reason, I pray for these signs. These words are spoken when the time for truth has arrived.

Regarding "no difference": the commentary states that this is the manifestation of the third auspicious sign. Because he previously made his vow, the King of his Mind reached the Tathāgata as its response;
sounds issued forth and flowers rained down amidst the music, and from within it, a voice proclaimed: "One who acts according to what they say."
It is so, it is so. The True Dharma is without lock; there is doubt regarding the true fruit, yet one should rely upon and study it.

It is said that upon seeing those wondrous flowers, they were filled with immeasurable joy. The commentary states: "The fourth [section] shows that the great assembly saw them together, as did the retinue of Śrīmālā."
All in the assembly beheld this event; their doubts and perplexities were extinguished, and their joy knew no bounds.

As for the words regarding the making of vows to reach the same destination as those who practice together, the commentary states: "The fifth is the simultaneous making of vows. There are two kinds of vows:
first, that we, the great multitude, may always be born together and never be separated; second, that if there are various practices [to be undertaken]..."

The practice is no different. It is said that the World-Honored One fully predicted [their attainment] exactly as they wished. The commentary states: this refers to the Tathāgata’s granting of permission.
Although there are two types of acceptance, these correspond to the second line of the first passage.

Below are two sections clarifying the teachings on the two types of vows: those for the distracted and those for the concentrated. Within these, the distracted comes first, followed by the concentrated. Within the section on the distracted, there are two parts:

first, Śrīmālā’s formulation of the vows; second, the Tathāgata’s praise. In the former, there are two sub-sections: first, a general statement regarding the purpose of formulating the vows; second, the specific formulation of the three vows.
The passage from "At that time, Śrīmālā [reached] infinite sentient beings" to the end is described as a general introduction. "I have already practiced this;

now I shall make a true vow to comfort sentient beings, so that they may be free from suffering and attain happiness, benefiting all living beings"—the three vows that follow are divided into three textual sections.
The section from "By these roots of goodness" to the "First Great Vow" is described as the aspiration for the True Dharma.
"Wisdom-vow" refers to the wisdom of expounding the teachings. Regarding the statement, "I shall attain the True Dharma," up to the second great vow, the commentary states:

Having previously generated the wisdom of the True Dharma, if one attains this vow, then throughout immeasurable kalpas, for the sake of all sentient beings, one will constantly preach the sublime Dharma, never having a mind of weariness, exhaustion, or anxiety. Regarding the statement, "I shall embrace and sustain," up to the third great vow:

The commentary states: Because one never tires of preaching the Dharma, regarding all that pertains to body, life, and wealth within the context of upholding the true Dharma, there is no mind of stinginess or regret;
thus, one is always able to protect and maintain the true Dharma without letting it be destroyed. "Protecting" (*hū*) means guarding, and "maintaining" (*dhṛ*) means supporting;
through this, the true Dharma is never forgotten or lost.
It is said that at that time, the World-Honored One immediately [spoke] from the "Excellence of Śrīmālā" down to the three great vows.

The commentary states: Regarding the second section, the Tathāgata’s praise is threefold: first, the teaching; second, the analogy; third, the application of the teaching to the case at hand. This is the first [the teaching].

Because you are able to give rise to these three vows, whose essence and function are vast and extensive, they are called "great. It is said: "Just as all forms enter entirely into the realm of space. The commentary states:
It is said: "This is an analogy. Just as the empty space can contain all colors, so too is this like a room; the metaphor of "removing" [defilements] is used because one does not perceive evil.
To say "thus" means that the Bodhisattva has reached the truly vast. The commentary states: "This is the application to the dharma.

The great vows, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, are all contained within the three [vows]. Because the essence and function of these three vows are expansive and broad, they are called "truly vast."

Within the section on the vows of meditative concentration (*samādhi-praṇidhāna*), there are two parts: first, the brief [exposition], and second, the extensive [exposition]. Within the brief exposition, there are four sections:
first, the request for instruction by Śrīmālā; second, the Tathāgata’s granting of permission; third, the formal exposition by Śrīmālā; and fourth, the Tathāgata’s praise.
The statement "At that time, Śrīmālā reached the truth of non-differentiation" is described as her initial request for the teaching.

Śrīmālā said: "Now, further sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, I again request [the teaching on] the Great Vow of Subduing. This shall certainly not be in vain. "Subduing" (*tiao*) refers to cultivating the wholesome; "subjugating" (*fu*) refers to breaking the unwholesome.
Alternatively, "subduing" refers to self-benefit, while "subjugating" refers to benefiting others. Or, it refers to abiding in the prior state of a mind characterized by outflows (*sāsrava*).

"Kiu. This means being interrupted by a mind characterized by signs (*nimitta*); it does not mean being tamed (*vinīta*). Here, it is clarified that true understanding free from signs is not interrupted by a mind characterized by signs;
therefore, it is called "tamed. Question: Regarding the three types of action (*karma*) mentioned above, none were preceded by the Buddha's presence.

Why is this particular instance alone entitled to such a name? Answer: There are two explanations. First, it is said that the three [types of] minds mentioned above belong to the preparatory stage (*prayoga*), whereas this [present case] belongs to the stage of abiding (*sthiti*). Thus...

"Regarding my own portion of wisdom, it does not rely on the Buddha; however, the practice of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) for upholding the True Dharma now requires deep aspiration and a far-reaching resolve, which is beyond my own realm.
It must necessarily rely upon the Buddha. The second [point] states: "The first chapter correctly elucidates the eternally abiding fruit of Buddhahood.

This is indeed a difficult point. To comply with your letter, I have recorded it in detail above. Once Śrīmālā had read it, she understood it accordingly without doubt, and thereupon she offered this praise:"
It is said: "Today, this chapter contains no record of the two types—conduct and vows. Śrīmālā was raised in seclusion, dwelling only within the deep inner palace;

she has not yet heard the holy instructions. Looking up toward the sky and facing the Buddha, she requests that you grant her the opportunity to speak of them. These conduct and vows are not the domain of ordinary or inferior knowledge."
Only a Buddha can realize this. Therefore, this sutra states: "The Tathāgata praises this upholding of the True Dharma;

it is that which all Buddhas of the three periods of time have collectively extolled and taught. Now I am likewise so; its merit is immeasurable. Thus, this single section alone receives the words of the Buddha.
It says: "The Buddha told Śrīmālā, 'Listen as you please and speak. The commentary states: Second.

The Buddha granted permission. "At your pleasure" means to follow one's own inclination; you may speak according to your will. "I now add three more" refers to the three types of action (*trīṇi karmāṇi*).
First is the manifestation of the teacherless body, which is the addition of the body. Second is the praise of Queen Śrīmālā’s speech, which gives rise to these two actions.
Regarding the mind, there are two aspects: volition (*cetanā*), which is the addition of the mind. Because she is now permitted to speak at her ease, it says: "Queen Śrīmālā said."
"The Buddha’s arrival at the state of True Suchness constitutes the Great Vow. The commentary states: The third section, the actual exposition, has three parts.

First, "The comprehensive inclusion," which simply means subsuming function back into essence. Second, from "That which is called" onwards, the actual presentation of the essence of the vow. Third, from "The comprehensive inclusion" onwards, the concluding praise of the excellence of the vow.
However, the general meaning is as follows: All the immeasurable vows of a bodhisattva are entirely contained within one great vow.
What is this? It is the vow to uphold the True Dharma (*saddharma-parigraha*). This includes all wholesome dharmas throughout the entire *dharmadhātu* without exception;
this is what is meant by "upholding. Because this vow is truly a great vow, it is praised among the praises of the Tathāgata.
Second: First, the Tathāgata’s praise; second, Śrīmālā’s further praise. Within the former, there are three parts: first, praising wisdom, which refers to two capacities;
second, citing all Buddhas of the three periods as testimony; third, taking one’s own practice as testimony. Within the first of these, there are two parts.
First, there is the praise of wisdom; second, the praise of the teaching. It is said that the Buddha praised Śrīmālā as being exceedingly profound and subtle.
The commentary states: "You possess wisdom and skillful means (*upāya*); these are not known by those of inferior capacity. They are exceedingly profound, subtle, and inconceivable.

Wisdom refers to ultimate wisdom (*jñāna*), while skillful means refers to provisional wisdom (*prajñā*). Ultimate wisdom illuminates reality, which is termed "profound"; provisional wisdom is skillful.
"Use" refers to subtlety; it may also mean that both types of wisdom are profound and skillful.
"I have understood what you have said after a long night" is a statement of praise for your exposition. You have long planted the roots of goodness.

Sentient beings of future generations—if they have not long planted the roots of goodness—others will be unable to understand what you have said. What you have said is extremely profound and difficult to fathom.

Therefore, it is said: "What you have said until now, and what you shall say. The commentary states: Having cited the Buddhas of the three periods as witnesses, this indicates that it is not only you who have begun to speak of this upholding of the True Dharma (*saddharmaparigraha*) now; rather, the Buddhas of the past three periods have already expounded it extensively.
It is further said: "I have now attained [the state] up to the upholding of the True Dharma. The commentary states: This is citing oneself as a witness. Why?
However, the Buddhas of the three periods have already spoken of this; since I attained unsurpassed *bodhi*, I too have constantly taught it. From here on, Śrīmālā further speaks in praise.
Within the preceding section, there are two parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation. According to the Sanskrit original, "wisdom" (*prajñā*) is mentioned first and "speech" (*vāk*) later;
the current translator has followed this version rather than relying on other regional texts. If one discusses this cause, it should be...
Because it is taught first as wisdom and subsequently as speech, there are two parts herein: first, the statement of the teaching; second, the statement of the wisdom.
The passage from "Thus have I spoken" up to "cannot reach its limit" is described as the statement of the teaching. This describes all the merits of upholding the True Dharma as thus taught;
if one wishes to exhaustively measure them, one cannot reach their limit. Among the thirty-two marks, this refers to the Brahma-voice.
Because its characteristics are most excellent, it is said that the Tathāgata’s wisdom and eloquence are likewise boundless.

The commentary states: How could the seven kinds of inexhaustible eloquence be fathomed by the mind? It asks, "For what reason? and answers, "Because it possesses supreme and great benefit. The commentary explains:
This refers to the merit and benefit of upholding the True Dharma, both of which are immeasurable. This concludes the brief exposition above.

Within the *Vaipulya* [section], there are two parts: first, the detailed exposition by Śrīmālā; second, the Tathāgata’s expression of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*). Within the former, there are two parts:
first, Śrīmālā receiving empowerment to provide the detailed exposition; second, attributing the merit to the Buddha. Within the former, there are three parts: first, Śrīmālā requesting the teaching.
First, the Buddha’s empowerment; second, the two Buddhas’ permission to speak; third, the actual exposition.

Regarding the passage from “Śrīmālā said to the Buddha” up to “the meaning of the vast,” the commentary states: this is the request. Regarding the passage “The Buddha said, ‘Speak,’ and she spoke,” the commentary states:
this is the permission. Within the actual exposition, there are two parts: first, a general indication that there are three [topics]; second, an extensive explanation based on that indication.
Regarding the statement from "Śrīmālā addressed the Buddha" up to "four thousand dharma-gates," the commentary states that this is a general summary.
Since it speaks of the vast meaning of embracing the true Dharma (*saddharmaparigraha*), what constitutes this? Now there are three meanings. The first is its vastness in producing the immeasurable.
Second, because it extensively accomplishes all Buddha-dharmas; third, because it extensively encompasses and contains the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates.
Possessing these three meanings is what is called the "vast meaning of upholding the true Dharma. In the explanation below, there are three parts.
Regarding the explanation of these three, for what reason do these three exist? The answer is: because one has previously made three kinds of great vows.
First, to attain right wisdom; this corresponds to the present immeasurable [teachings]. Second, to preach for the sake of sentient beings with a tireless mind;
this corresponds to the present eighty-four thousand dharma-gates, which is the third [vow]. Third, to protect and uphold the true Dharma; this corresponds to the present second [vow].
"All Buddha-dharmas" [refers to the title]. The four characters "Cloud-Water Kṣitigarbha" explain the "immeasurable" mentioned above.

Question: Why are the former [sections] not mentioned in the heading, yet appear in the subsequent detailed explanation?
Question: In the summary, the fruit is indicated. For the treatise, it must first mature the faculties and only then gather sentient beings;

this serves as the basis for the sequence of the preceding meaning. In the detailed explanation below, since the fruit arises from itself according to the sequence of its causes, it cannot be further explained.
In the explanation of "Immeasurable" (apramāṇa), there are four meanings: first, like clouds, because internal virtues are fused; second, like water, because others are satisfied;
third, like the earth, because the benefit of gathering [beings] is sufficient; and fourth, like a treasure-trove, because it contains all things in their entirety.

Question: Why are these four metaphors arranged in this specific order? Answer: At the beginning of a kalpa, clouds are able to cover everywhere; thus, clouds serve as a metaphor for the mind that rains down the waters of the sun. When the waters dry up...

The earth serves as a metaphor; that within the earth there are treasuries serves as a further metaphor. The preceding section has two parts: first the metaphor, and second the application to the Dharma.

The passage beginning with "For example, at the time of the initial formation of a kalpa" and ending with "and various kinds of jewels" is the description of the metaphor. This refers to the completion of the twenty intermediate kalpas of emptiness.
From above downward, the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) is formed, reaching as far as the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*cāturmahārājakāyika*).
Within the Yāma Heaven, great clouds and mists gather, displacing two thousand worlds. From within these clouds, winds arise from both sides; the wind below becomes firm and solid.
It circulates around the four directions and gradually rains down again. There is water struck by wind, and there is a golden wheel as the foundation of the earth.
Upon this earth-wheel, there is further water that forms an ocean; because it rises upward, it is named Mount Sumeru. There are seven golden mountains.
Because the four great continents arise [therein], within the great clouds there are produced immeasurable fruits and five kinds of rain, as well as various treasures—namely, the four...

By way of their colors: the east is of gold, the south of lapis lazuli, the west of silver, and the north of crystal. The east is named Vijaya (Victorious Body) because its inhabitants have handsome and dignified countenances;
the south is named Jambūdvīpa (Jambu Island) because it is named after the *jambu* tree; the west is named Godānīya (Cow-Trade) because they use cattle for commerce;
the north is named Kuru (Uttarakuru) because the land is situated at the northern side. These are provided as illustrations. Thus is the summary.
"Receiving the rain of the roots of supreme goodness" is described as "the Dharma. From this, by embracing the True Dharma, there arises the rain of the roots of goodness;
immeasurable meritorious rewards accordingly arise from these two. In this current passage, the order is not followed, placing the effect before the cause.
Within the second [section], there are two parts: first the analogy, and later the Dharma. It says, "Furthermore, it is like at the beginning of a kalpa..."

"At the time of completion, it reaches various kinds of continents. [The commentary] states: "This is an illustration. "The treasury of the trichiliocosm" refers to that which is transformed by a single Buddha and sustained by water.

There are four hundred *koṭis* of various kinds of continents. (Apart from this trichiliocosm, there are four hundred *koṭis*. The categories differ: sometimes one million is called a *koṭi*, and sometimes ten million is called a *koṭi*. To avoid being overly expansive, yet not too concise, we take ten million as a *koṭi*. This is neither too much nor too little; thus it receives the name "one hundred *koṭis*. The name is not different. **Sanskrit Reconstruction:** *niṣpattikāle nānāvidhadvīpān prāpnoti.* Vyākhyānam āha: dṛṣṭāntopanyāsaḥ. Koṭi-prakārā bhinnāḥ: kadācit lakṣaṃ koṭir ucyate, kadācit daśa-lakṣaṃ koṭir ucyate. Na vistara-gāmi, na saṃkṣepa-gāmi;

kintu madhyamaṃ daśa-lakṣaṃ koṭim gṛhṇīmaḥ. Nāpi bahvī, nāpy alpā; śata-koṭi-saṃjñāṃ labhate. Saṃjñā na viśiṣyate. **English Translation:** "At the time of its formation, it extends to various types of continents. The commentary says: "This is an example. "The matrix of the three-thousandfold world system" means that which is emanated by a single Buddha and supported by water. There are four hundred *koṭis* of various types of continents. (Excluding this trichiliocosm, there are another four hundred *koṭis*. The categories of these numbers vary: sometimes a million is termed a *koṭi*, and sometimes ten million is termed a *koṭi*. Thus, it is neither excessive nor deficient, and it receives the designation of "one hundred *koṭis*. The name remains consistent.)

One Sumeru has four continents. Since there are ten billion Sumerus, this refers to the ten billion sets of four continents—that is, one hundred and forty billion. The phrase "thus encompassing" up to "all emerge from within" is described as referring to the Dharma.

Regarding the phrase "thus embracing... up to the most supreme": 1. **General Presentation of the Common Illustration:** Just as the four kinds of treasures are embraced by the earth, so too are these four kinds of bodhisattvas embraced by the bodhisattva stages (*bhūmi*). 2. **Posing of a Question:** Why is it said that they are embraced? 3. **Specific Commonality:** Because they are the basis for the arising of the four kinds of bodhisattvas. 4. **Conclusion:** Therefore, it is said they are embraced. Regarding the phrase "thus embracing... up to the most supreme": this refers to the fact that the four kinds of bodhisattvas are embraced by the four bodhisattva stages, beginning from the stage of joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) up to the stage of the cloud of dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*). "Great Treasure. [The commentary] states: This is a general correspondence. "What are the four? [The commentary] states: This is the raising of the question.
"From 'embracing the True Dharma' to 'bestowing the Mahāyāna. [The commentary] states: This is a specific correspondence. "Thus obtaining the Great [Treasure]... up to embracing the True Dharma.
[The commentary] states: This is the concluding text. Within it there are two parts. The first concludes that sentient beings obtain the treasure, revealing that—by means of—...
"Upholding the True Dharma. Second, "binding the great jewel," which is precisely upholding the True Dharma. This can be understood according to the text.
Below this, the text explains the inclusion of the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates; therein are two parts. First, the general is used to clarify the specific teachings.

Second, by means of the general being identical to the particular practice, it is said: "The World-Honored One’s bestowing and receiving... is itself the upholding of the True Dharma. The commentary states:
Taking the general as identical to the particular, and the particular again as identical [to the general], because they are mutually identical, their essence is not different.

From this point downward, there are three sections within the distinct exposition: first, the heading; second, the explanation; and third, the conclusion. Regarding the statement, "The World-Honored One is no different [from]...
up to 'this is a pāramitā,'" the commentary states that this is a general heading. According to the preceding teaching, it should have been stated:
"The World-Honored One’s embracing of the True Dharma and the one who embraces the True Dharma are no different from the pāramitās, etc. However, the translators could not bear the prolixity.
The extensive [explanation] has already been concluded above; the subsequent text abbreviates it, merely stating that there is no difference from the *pāramitās* and so forth.

Within the separate explanation, there are two parts: first, the inquiry; second, the explanation. As for the phrase "Why is it that... up to the son or daughter of good family," it refers to the inclusion [of these categories].

The commentary states: This is the inquiry and record. The phrase "sons of good family" and so forth encompasses the six perfections below. Within the first six perfections, the text is divided into six sections.
From here on, in the exposition of *dāna* (generosity), there are three parts: first, the designation of those to be converted;

second, maturing them through generosity and so forth, which constitutes the gathering of others through shared practice; third, the conclusion of one’s own practice as the meaning of a *pāramitā*. It says:
Regarding those who should be matured through giving: the commentary states that the first [section] indicates those to be converted.

Within the gathering of those with similar conduct, there are three parts: first, the Bodhisattva’s own practice of giving; second, from "protecting their intentions" onwards, gathering others through giving;

and third, from "those whom they have matured" onwards, clarifying the causal stage of the virtues of the beings to be converted. As for the phrase "matured through giving," up to... [text continues].
"Relinquishing the limbs and members of the body. Commentary: This is the first, the Bodhisattva’s own practice of giving (*dāna*).

"Protecting their intentions and bringing them to maturity. Commentary: This is the second, gathering others through giving. "That which they accomplish and establish as the True Dharma (*saddharma*).
Commentary: This is the third, the virtue of the sentient beings being transformed. "This is called the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). Commentary: [End of commentary.]

This third section is the conclusion. Regarding the remaining five perfections below, they are all as in the case of generosity; they cannot be described in detail here, and one should understand them by analogy.

Within the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla*), there are three parts. As for the statement, "one should accomplish [the goal] through ethical discipline," the commentary states: this indicates the object to be transformed.
"Guarding" refers to protecting the six sense bases and maintaining the four correct modes of deportment. The commentary states: this is the Bodhisattva’s own upholding of the precepts.

"Bringing others to maturity by guarding them" means gathering others through the precepts. The commentary states: this is the response regarding those to be converted. "That which brings them to maturity, leading to the establishment of the True Dharma," and so forth. The commentary states: this is the third conclusion. *Note:

The term "至正" (zhì zhèng) is interpreted here as "correct" (zhèng), referring to the four *īryāpathas* (modes of deportment). The phrase "所化答" (*suǒ huà dá*) is interpreted as the "response regarding those to be converted" (*vineya-prativacana*).*

Regarding the three types within the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), it should be understood by analogy. As for the statement, "One should bring them to maturity through patience," the commentary states: this indicates those to be converted. As for the statement, "If those sentient beings reach the point where their facial expressions do not change," the commentary states: this refers to the Bodhisattva’s own practice of patience. If there are sentient beings who revile and insult one in various ways, yet one remains free from anger, this is the patience of enduring enmity and harm (*āghātakhama-kṣānti*). As for the phrase, "with a mind of benefit" (*anugraha-citta*): The commentary states: this refers to the patience of benefiting others (*parānugraha-kṣānti*). It means that even when sentient beings revile and insult one in various ways, one maintains a mind of benefit toward them, thinking, "May they attain happiness. Furthermore, it means that even when sentient beings revile and insult one in various ways, one maintains a mind of benefit toward them, thinking, "May they attain liberation. This is called the patience of benefiting others. Regarding the phrase, "even if one's body is cut into pieces": the commentary states: this refers to the patience of accepting suffering (*duḥkhādhivāsana-kṣānti*). It means that even if one's body is cut into pieces, one does not give rise to anger; rather, one thinks, "I have obtained great benefit, as I am able to endure such suffering. This is called the patience of accepting suffering. Regarding the phrase, "if one gives rise to anger": the commentary states: this refers to the patience of reflecting on the Dharma (*dharmanidhyāna-kṣānti*). It means that even if sentient beings revile and insult one in various ways, one reflects on the Dharma and does not give rise to anger. This is called the patience of reflecting on the Dharma. Regarding the phrase, "if one gives rise to a mind of resentment": the commentary states: this refers to the patience of reflecting on causes and conditions (*hetupratyaya-nidhyāna-kṣānti*). It means that even if sentient beings revile and insult one in various ways, one reflects on causes and conditions and does not give rise to a mind of resentment. This is called the patience of reflecting on causes and conditions. Regarding the phrase, "if one gives rise to a mind of pride": the commentary states: this refers to the patience of reflecting on emptiness (*śūnyatā-nidhyāna-kṣānti*). It means that even if sentient beings revile and insult one in various ways, one reflects on emptiness and does not give rise to a mind of pride. This is called the patience of reflecting on emptiness. Within the following section on diligence (*vīrya*), there are also three parts. Regarding the statement, "those who should be matured through diligence," the commentary says: this indicates those to be converted (*vineya*).
Regarding the statement, "toward those sentient beings, even during the four modes of deportment (*iryāpatha*)," the commentary says: this refers to the Bodhisattva’s own practice of diligence.

Regarding the statement, "not giving rise to indolence," this is the diligence of donning armor (*saṃnāha-vīrya*). Regarding the phrase, "giving rise to the mind of great aspiration," this is the diligence of gathering wholesome qualities (*kuśala-saṃgrāhaka-vīrya*).
This is progress. Regarding "the first," it refers to the diligence of benefiting and bringing happiness. The phrase "protecting their intentions, etc. is explained as being encompassed by diligence.
The phrase "that which has been matured, etc. is explained as the benefit for those to be converted. The section beginning with "this is called," etc., follows.
The commentary states: This is the third conclusion. From here on, within the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*), there are also three parts.

Regarding the statement, "One should bring [beings] to maturity through meditation," the commentary states: this indicates those to be converted. Regarding the statement, "For those sentient beings, until the end, one does not forget or lose [the path]," the commentary states:
this refers to the bodhisattva’s practice of meditation. "With an undisturbed mind" means because of abiding in meditative concentration (*samādhi*); that is, within the four dhyānas.
It is the dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*). "With a mind not directed outward" refers to the meditative absorption that brings forth [supernormal powers];

for it is able to bring forth immeasurable supernormal powers because the mind constantly takes the internal as its object. "The first right mindfulness," and so forth, refers to the meditative absorption that accomplishes tasks;
for it is able to mature all sentient beings and does not forget for a long time what has been done or said. Thus it is called...
Regarding "protecting their minds" and so forth, the commentary states: this refers to gathering them through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

Regarding "those whom they have matured" and so forth, the commentary states: this refers to the benefit for those to be converted. Regarding "this is called" and so forth, the commentary states: this is the third conclusion.

Below this, there are likewise three [sections] concerning wisdom (*prajñā*). Regarding "those who should be matured by means of wisdom," the commentary states: this indicates those to be converted. Regarding... [text continues].
"Those sentient beings reach the various arts and crafts. [Commentary: This describes the bodhisattva’s own practice of wisdom.

It shows that the bodhisattva possesses the study of the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) in order to bring sentient beings to maturity. Regarding the phrase "protecting their intentions," [the commentary] states: this refers to gathering them through wisdom.

Regarding the phrase "those whom they have matured," [the commentary] states: this refers to the benefit for those to be converted. Regarding the section beginning with "this is called," etc. [the commentary follows].
The commentary states: This is the third conclusion.
Regarding the passage from "Therefore, the World-Honored One" to "this is the pāramitā," the commentary states: This is the third concluding text.
From here on, regarding the second [section], "attaining all Buddha-dharmas" refers to the third of the three great vows mentioned in the preceding text.
This concerns the upholding of the True Dharma. The text is divided into three parts: first, the request for the teaching; second, the Buddha’s consent; third, the actual exposition.
The passage "World-Honored One, I now, relying on the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, shall further explain the great meaning" describes the request for the teaching.

Furthermore, after the Buddha has bestowed his triple empowerment, [the speaker says] "I shall now further explain," which describes the Buddha’s consent. When the Buddha says, "Speak," it describes the Buddha’s permission. The Buddha says, "You..."

It is appropriate to explain further according to the circumstances. From this point downward, the main body of the text consists of three parts: first, showing that the Dharma is identical to the person;

second, explaining the reason for the aforementioned [identity], clarifying that there are three distinct aspects; and third, clarifying the protection [of the teaching]. Within the first part, there are two sections:
first, clarifying that the person and the Dharma are non-different; and second, clarifying their mutual identity. This begins with "Śrīmālā addressed the Buddha" up to "receiving and sustaining."

"Right Dharma. [The commentary] states: "To clarify that there is no difference" means that the "person" (pudgala) is merely a designation; it refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). There is no distinct person apart from these;

rather, because a person is a composite designation formed by grasping at distinct dharmas, the practice of upholding the Right Dharma as a distinct activity is itself the one who upholds the Right Dharma.
Since this composite lacks an intrinsic nature apart from the distinct dharmas, it is called "no difference. Thus, it is said: "upholding the Right Dharma..."
"The Dharma reaching [the person] is itself the upholding of the True Dharma. The commentary states: "To clarify means that there is no difference.
Since it is said that a son of good family who upholds the True Dharma is himself the upholding of the True Dharma, we know that the Dharma is identical to that person.

From this point downward, there are three sections explaining the underlying reasons. First, relying on the preceding reasons, the momentum is established to give rise to [the following], clarifying that person and phenomena are mutually identical;
this section has three parts. Second, it clarifies the relinquishing of three and the attaining of three. Third, it provides a summary. Within the first of these, there are two parts:
first, the posing of the question; second, the formal explanation. Regarding the phrase "For what reason" (*kasmāt*), the commentary states: [The question asks] "What is the basis for..."?
Because there is no difference in the upholding of the True Dharma (*saddharma-parigraha*), it is further stated that they are "identical.
The following passage is the response. It says: "If one upholds the True Dharma... up to abandoning the three kinds of divisions. [The commentary] states: This is an explanation.

For what reason can it be known that they are identical to the Dharma and to persons? Because they are able to abandon the three distinct types. Since they are known to be identical, what are these [three]? From here below—
The detailed explanation consists of three parts: first, the inquiry; second, the brief answer; and third, the detailed explanation. Regarding the phrase "What are the three?":

the commentary states that this is the question. Since it has been said that there are three, which ones are they? The phrase "namely, body, life, and wealth" is the brief answer. The commentary states that this is the summary response.
"Sacrificing the body" refers to using one's own person to assist in the work of transformation, not begrudging one's effort and labor, and so forth. "Sacrificing life" [refers to...]

This refers to being able to rescue others from various sufferings without regard for one’s own body or life. "Relinquishing wealth" means being able to completely give away both internal and external possessions.
To explain these three points individually, the text is divided into three sections. Within the first section, there are two parts:
first, clarifying the arousal of constancy and so forth; second, clarifying the five virtues. The passage beginning with "Good son, until the end of saṃsāra," etc., describes [the first part].
It is said: "This clarifies that delusion and awakening are equal. To speak of "birth and death" refers to defiled bondage; "the posterior limit" refers to returning to cessation.
To say they are "equal" means these two are without difference. Why is this so? Because True Suchness (Tathatā) is the basis for both delusion and awakening.
If one possesses wisdom and attains realization, it constitutes the nirvana of the posterior limit; if one possesses ignorance and is deluded, then...
Birth and death arise in succession; this is because that which lacks *nirvāṇa* is called defiled bondage.

The statement "departing from old age, sickness, and death, one reaches the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata" is explained as clarifying five virtues: first, the virtue of departing from old age, sickness, and death; second, the virtue of being indestructible and eternally abiding;
third, the virtue of being without change or transformation; fourth, the virtue of inconceivable merit; and fifth, the virtue of the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata.

Regarding the two aspects of relinquishing life (*jīvitotsarga*): the first clarifies that there is no difference [between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa], as can be understood from the previous explanation beginning with "because they are equal.

The second clarifies the five virtues. What are these? It says, "As for relinquishing life," etc. The commentary states: this clarifies that there is no difference between birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and nirvāṇa.
It says, "Ultimately departing from death" up to "the profound and vast Dharma. The commentary states: this clarifies the five virtues. First, ultimate...
1. Freedom from death; 2. Attainment of the boundless; 3. Eternal abiding; 4. Inconceivable merit; 5.
Thorough penetration of all profound and vast teachings. Within the relinquishing of wealth, there are two parts: first, clarifying non-duality through the phrase "because of equality," etc.;

second, clarifying the six virtues. What are they? It says: "The relinquishing of wealth [extends to] the limits of birth and death," and so forth. The commentary states: This clarifies birth and death.
Nirvana is without distinction. It is said that one attains what is not shared with any sentient beings, up to the most excellent offerings.
The commentary states: this clarifies six virtues: first, the virtue of non-commonality; second, the virtue of being inexhaustible and undiminished;

third, the virtue of ultimate accomplishment; fourth, the virtue of inconceivability; fifth, the virtue of being fully endowed with merit; and sixth, the virtue of receiving offerings. It says: "The World-Honored One is like..."
"This is that which is to be gazed upon with reverence. [The commentary] states: This is the conclusion.
It says, "The World-Honored One, and furthermore, good sons, etc. [The commentary] states: The third section clarifies the capacity for protection. Within this, there are two parts.
First, when the True Dharma is about to perish, the fourfold assembly becomes discordant. Second, one enters into reconciliation with them by means of an upright mind.
Regarding the statement, "Furthermore, O World-Honored One, good sons," and so forth: this refers to the first section. "Factionalism" (pungdang) refers to mutual instigation and delusion.
"Contention" (*saṃghāta*) refers to the settlement of disputes between two parties; it is called "destruction" because of such contention. It is said to be "dispersion" because of factionalism.
Furthermore, it is said that factionalism is the mental action (*manas-karman*), contention is the verbal action (*vāk-karman*), and dispersion is the physical action (*kāya-karman*).

Regarding the statement, "By means of being free from flattery and crookedness, one enters among the ranks of the Dharma-friends," the commentary states: this clarifies the harmonizing of others. Within this, there are two parts:
first, clarifying reconciliation through not begrudging body or life; second, being recorded by the Tathāgata. This refers to the former.
This involves five kinds of mental states that can harmonize those who are in conflict, dispute, or discord. The first is a body free from flattery and crookedness.
1. Karmic action; 2. verbal karmic action of a non-deceptive mind; 3. mental karmic action of non-illusory artifice. The three above differ from evil. 4.
Mental karmic action of delighting in the True Dharma; 5. verbal karmic action of upholding the True Dharma;

bodily karmic action of entering the ranks of the Dharma-friends. The three below are likewise virtuous. Because one is constrained and hindered by these three [evil] minds, one enters [into suffering].

"Among the ranks of the Dharma-friends" means not entering among the ranks of heterodox followers. "To enter the ranks of the Dharma-friends" refers to reaching the point of receiving a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
The commentary states: this is what the Tathāgata has predicted.

He said, "World-Honored One, I have seen the ultimate and fully know and see it. The commentary states: This second passage dedicates merit to the Buddha, clarifying that the Buddha serves as the witness and demonstrating that the Dharma is worthy of practice.

Regarding the second section on the Tathāgata’s sympathetic joy (*anumodana*), there are two parts. First, the narrator introduces the passage to clarify that the Buddha gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy.
Second, the actual clarification of the mind of sympathetic joy. The text states: "At that time, the World-Honored One... gave rise to a mind of sympathetic joy. The commentary says:

This passage from the sūtra’s compiler generally indicates the Buddha’s intention of rejoicing (*anumodana*). Since he is able to embrace and sustain the True Dharma (*saddharma*), this constitutes the power of great diligence (*vīrya*).
"Diligence" (*jing*) means purity; "advancement" (*jin*) means fierce valor. Therefore, it is called diligence.
Within this section on Right Joy (*samyak-prīti*), there are three parts: first, clarifying the greatness of the power of diligence; second, exhorting Śrīmālā to embrace [the teaching];
and third, citing oneself as an example. Within the first part, there are three: first, the strong man; second, the bull king; and third, Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains.
Within the section on the strong man, there are two: first, presenting the analogy; second, applying it to the Dharma. It says: "In this way, Śrīmālā... [endures] great suffering."
"Pain. The commentary states: Since you possess the great power of diligence in upholding and receiving the True Dharma, you cannot be subdued;
it is like a powerful wrestler who, by exerting a slight force with his hand upon another's body, causes that person to experience endless suffering.

This refers to how Queen Śrīmālā caused Māra to suffer distress. The commentary states that this is a synthesis. There are two parts: citing the remainder and providing an inverse explanation. This is the first.

When a bodhisattva understands and possesses this upholding of the True Dharma (*saddharma-parigraha*), they are able to eliminate the four māras. Because of this small power, the various māras retreat and disperse.
Cultivating roots of goodness for one’s own benefit is termed "a small portion," yet because of this slight upholding of the True Dharma, all māras experience sorrow and suffering.

Regarding the phrase "I do not see" and below, the commentary states that this is an inverted explanation; it means that he does not see the ordinary beings or those of the two vehicles who possess minor virtues as being subject to suffering.
This is a minor virtue. Within the analogy of the bull-king (*go-rāja*), there are two parts: first, the presentation of the simile; second, the application to the dharma.
The phrase "Furthermore, like a bull-king who surpasses all other bulls" is explained as clarifying the simile. Now, this bull-king possesses five characteristics:

namely, the sharpness of his horns, his broad and well-proportioned body, his majestic appearance, his dignified gait, and his superiority among all cattle; for these reasons, he is called a "bull-king. As for the phrase "like... [the text continues].
"This is the Great Vehicle because it is supremely vast. The commentary states: All roots of goodness have three distinctions.

Now, these roots of goodness that are embraced here surpass the roots of goodness of the other two vehicles; they are called "a small portion" because they cite only the single virtue of benefiting others.
Why is this so? Because the Mahāyāna is vast and great. Within the King of Mountains, there are two parts: first, the presentation of the analogy;
second, the application of the analogy to the Dharma. It says, "Furthermore, like Sumeru, the King of Mountains, which excels all other mountains. The commentary states:
However, among the seven concentric mountain ranges surrounding Mount Sumeru, this one is the most preeminent and is thus called the "King of Mountains.
Regarding the statement that such a great assembly is "vast," the commentary explains that there are two ways of gathering [disciples]:

first, not relinquishing body, life, or wealth—referring to Bodhisattvas prior to the stages (bhūmi) and those in the first stage; second, relinquishing body, life, and wealth while further being able to gather and uphold the True Dharma.

Because they are bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*), it is said that they surpass the roots of goodness of bodhisattvas in the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) of the Great Vehicle who have not yet renounced body, life, and wealth;
even these do not equal the roots of goodness of those on the stages, let alone the goodness of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*).
Therefore, it says, "let alone the two vehicles. Why is this? Because the Great Vehicle is vast and expansive. Question: Why must there necessarily be three kinds?

Is this a metaphor? The answer is that there are five interpretations. First, it is said: The preceding passage speaks of "embracing all immeasurable Buddha-dharmas," which refers to the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates.
Here, the "wrestler" represents the immeasurable; the "bull-king" represents the embracing of the four thousand;
and the "Sumeru king" refers to all Buddha-dharmas. Second, it is said: There are three kinds of practice, namely, [the practice of] detachment... [text continues].

[The first] says: "Evil" refers to abandoning evil conduct; "benefiting sentient beings" refers to the practice of benefiting others; and "gathering what is wholesome" refers to the practice of gathering virtues. Now, the "wrestler" represents the abandonment of evil conduct; the "bull king" represents the practice of benefiting sentient beings;
and the "Sumeru mountain king" represents the practice of gathering what is wholesome. A third interpretation says: Because there are three vehicles, the "wrestler" surpasses the *śrāvakas*;
the "bull king" brings forth the *pratyekabuddhas*; and the "mountain king" brings forth those of the seventh stage. A fourth interpretation says: The Buddha possesses... [text ends].

1. Because he possesses the three bodies (*trikāya*). 2. Because his five causes involve the transcendence of the three delusions (*trivisaṃyojana*). 3. Because his functions involve the possession of the three insights (*traividya*).

4. Because he is able to eliminate the three poisons (*triviṣa*). 5. Because he is able to cultivate the three trainings (*triśikṣā*). 6. Because he is able to emerge from the three abodes (*tristhāna*). 7. Because he is forever free from the three miserable realms (*tridurgati*). 8.

A strong man (*mallika*) is taken as a metaphor for excellence in strength. 9. A bull king (*go-rāja*) is taken as a metaphor for excellence in external appearance. 10. A mountain king (*parvata-rāja*) is taken as a metaphor for excellence in substance. Furthermore, it is said that the strong man is a metaphor for [the Buddha].
"Victorious over the Māras; superior to the two vehicles like a bull-king; and superior to the earth before it was shaped by the king of mountains. It continues:
"Therefore, Śrīmālā, you should embrace [beings] up to establishing them. The commentary states: This is the second exhortation to study. Within it, there are two parts.
The first section clarifies the exhortation for Śrīmālā to expound the teaching; the second clarifies the benefits of such exposition. This is the first [section].

Now, there are three distinct capacities among sentient beings: first, the lowest; second, the middling; and third, the superior. To speak of the "Bodhisattva" (kai-shi) refers to the strongman of the lowest capacity.
To speak of "instructing others" refers to the ox-king of the middling capacity. To speak of "establishing" refers to the mountain-king of the superior capacity.
Furthermore, there are many other triads as described above. Regarding the passage from "Thus the Śrīmālā" to "such great fruit," the commentary states that this clarifies the benefits:
bestowing the Śrāvaka vehicle is called "great benefit"; bestowing the Pratyekabuddha fruit upon the "wrestler" is called "great merit";
and bestowing the Mahāyāna fruit upon the "bull king" is called "great fruit. As for the "mountain king," furthermore—
There are three further [passages]. These may be understood by analogy with what precedes.
Regarding the statement, "Śrīmālā, as for me, [I have reached] the limit of the ultimate," the commentary states: This third [section] cites the Buddha’s own words from below to provide proof.
Within this, there are two parts: first, the difficulty of exhausting [the description of] this; second, the difficulty [of describing its] boundless merit.
This is the first part. The Buddha said: "This upholding of the True Dharma is difficult to exhaust even if explained throughout many *saṃghakalpas*.
Not only is it difficult to reach the end of its explanation, but its merit is likewise immeasurable. Why is this? It is because Śrīmālā has reached boundless merit. The commentary states:
This concludes the clarification that the merits are boundless. The preceding four chapters have completed the exposition on practice;

from here on is the fifth section, which clarifies the fruit. This contains two parts: first, the Buddha’s exhortation to speak; second, Śrīmālā receiving his power and formally presenting her discourse.

Regarding the passage from "The Buddha told Śrīmālā" up to "the upholding of the True Dharma," the commentary states: The Buddha exhorted her through speech. There are three types of such exhortation—namely, those of body, speech, and mind—as fully detailed above. Question: In the preceding four chapters, the Tathāgata did not offer exhortation; rather, Śrīmālā spoke for herself. Why, then, does the Buddha here provide exhortation through speech? Answer: In the preceding four practices, she had already cultivated and studied them. [However, regarding this practice, she has not yet done so. Therefore, the Buddha now provides exhortation. Furthermore, because the True Dharma is difficult to uphold, he encourages her to do so. Moreover, although she previously spoke of the Dharma, she had not yet spoken of the person who upholds it. Now, having explained the Dharma, he explains the person who upholds it. Furthermore, because the True Dharma is subtle and profound, he encourages her to uphold it. Finally, because the True Dharma is the most supreme among all dharmas, he encourages her to uphold it. Thus, there are five reasons why the Buddha provides exhortation here. The intended answer is as follows: The Mahāyāna is the general; the general can contain the particular, and it is for this reason that it gives rise to the three vehicles and so forth.

There are two parts: first, the presentation of the simile; second, the application to the Dharma. Regarding the passage "The World-Honored One is like Anavatapta," etc., the commentary states that this presents the simile.
As for "Anavatapta," it means "Cool," because it is free from all heat. This name is an abbreviation; it should properly be called Lake Anavatapta.
It is located south of Gandhamādana Mountain and north of the Snowy Mountains (Himavat), with a depth of fifty *yojanas* and a square [extent].
It is also like this. Its banks are likewise fifty *yojana*s high. Except for those who have attained supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), no one can go there.
From this lake issue four great rivers: the Gaṅgā in the south, the Sindhu in the north, the Sītā in the west, and the Vakṣu in the east.
Having emerged as these [rivers] such as the Ox-head, each flows around the lake once before entering the oceans of the four directions. These four rivers thus flow forth.
Reaching fifty *yojanas*, each is divided into five. There are four rivers. Why, then, are eight great rivers mentioned here? Answer:
In other sūtras, the "four" refers to the primary [rivers]. Furthermore, another sūtra speaks of twenty rivers, which are all combined and mentioned at the end.
The "eight" mentioned here refers to this specific sūtra. On the southern side, the river is divided into five branches; furthermore, others are taken...
The three fundamental directions are called the Eight Rivers. In the south, one takes the end and discards the beginning; for the others, one takes the beginning and not the end.

The training in morality consists merely of dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*) and cannot sever the afflictions (*kleśa*). Only concentration and wisdom can eliminate them.

In this present passage, following the sequence for severing the afflictions, the training in morality is mentioned last, preceded by concentration and wisdom, because these two—concentration and wisdom—are capable of severing the afflictions and cultivating the wholesome. Thus it is named.
"Abiding" is called cessation (*nirodha*). Because of abiding, wholesome dharmas arise; because of cessation, all afflictions are exhausted.

Commentary. Within the commentary, there are two parts: first, the inquiry; second, the explanation. "For what reason? constitutes the inquiry. Within the explanation, there are three sections. The explanation of those three trainings consists of three textual passages.
The phrase "the True Dharma abides," etc., the commentary states, explains "abiding. This is because it encompasses both the trainings of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
The phrase "the True Dharma perishes," etc., the commentary states, explains "perishing. This is because it encompasses both trainings. The phrase "pāramitā," etc. [is the third].

Regarding *Prātimokṣa* and so forth: the commentary states that this explains the training in the precepts (*śīla-śikṣā*). Within this, there are two parts: first, explaining that *pāra* and *vinaya* are no different;
second, clarifying the renunciation and reception of full ordination (*upasampadā*). It is said that the term *prātimokṣa* refers to the first [part] as being distinct [in name].
The commentary states: "This clarifies that they are not different. Although these two differ in their breadth and brevity, their essence is not distinct; both equally clarify the precepts.

Regarding the study of the meaning [of the Vinaya]: within the explanation of renouncing the household life and receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), there are three parts. First, the correct understanding of the *vinaya*, which is itself the Mahāyāna training.
Second, clarifying why the preceding [sections] conclude by returning to the topic of renouncing the household life and receiving full ordination.

Third, citing the Arhats as witnesses to prove that there is no difference [between the two]. It is said that "the *vinaya* extends up to the reception of full ordination. The commentary states: this explains the *vinaya*. Regarding...
This section has two parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation. Within the explanation, there are two parts: first, the inquiry; second, the exposition.

The statement "the *vinaya* refers to those who study the Mahāyāna" is the heading, as it clarifies that [the *vinaya*] serves as a skillful means for the Mahāyāna and ultimately returns to its source.
The phrase "Why is this so? initiates the inquiry. The passage "Because one goes forth under the Buddha and receives full ordination" provides the explanation for why this is so.
Because the fruits of training in the three vehicles arise by following the Buddha’s own training, they constitute Mahāyāna training.

The statement "therefore it is called 'Great'" up to "receiving full ordination" is explained as follows: this describes the reason for being "mounted upon" (the vehicle), concluding with the point that one leaves the household life and receives full ordination.
Although the fruits arising later differ, they ultimately all return to the Mahāyāna; thus, these six dharmas are taught for the sake of the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, by what means is it known that [they] have attained [this]? It says, "Therefore, the Arhats, etc. This answers the aforementioned reason.
This third point cites the Arhats as evidence. Within this, there are two parts: first, the thesis statement; second, the explanation. The phrase "Therefore, the Arhats, etc.

is stated as the presentation of the core tenet (*mūla*). Regarding the person who is an Arhat, they do not possess the capacity to leave the household life (*pravrajyā*) on their own; they require...
"Because they rely on the Buddha. Furthermore, it says: "Apart from the Mahāyāna, there are no arhats who can leave the household life on their own; one must rely on the Mahāyāna.
Since it is stated here that even those who are like the rhinoceros-horn [pratyekabuddhas] see the Buddha, it follows that only the Buddhas naturally attain the precepts.
As for the question, "Why is this so?"—the commentary explains that there are two parts: first, the inquiry, and second, the explanation.
This is the inquiry. It states: "Because an Arhat relies upon [the Buddha] to receive full ordination. The commentary says: This explains the reason.

An Arhat must rely on the Tathāgata for such matters as leaving the household life; therefore, one should know that the six dharmas are for the sake of the Mahāyāna, as they explain the ultimate return to the source.
Regarding the inclusion within the second illumination on the results, there are two parts: first, a brief opening of two chapters; second, a brief and extensive explanation of the preceding chapter.
The statement, "The Arhat has fear," is described as the brief opening of the two chapters. First is the chapter on taking refuge in the Buddha.

"Because the dharmas of form have not yet been exhausted, there is a place of return. This clarifies the failure of the mind. Second is the chapter on "having fear," which serves as an antidote for those who have not yet reached the fifth stage (*bhūmi*) and still dwell in fear;
this clarifies the failure of practice. For this reason, even an Arhat must still rely upon the Buddha, as they still possess fear—this is the statement of the thesis.
In the subsequent explanation, there are two parts: first, a brief explanation of the two chapters; second, [the detailed explanation]. The letter "A" [marks the beginning].

Below the section on the Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas, two chapters are explained in detail. Within the brief exposition, there are two parts: first, the chapter on "Terror" is explained; second, from "Why is this?
World-Honored One, based upon the unique basis... onwards, the chapter on "Taking Refuge" is explained. Within the former [the chapter on Terror], there are three sections:
first, the Dharma (the teaching); second, the analogy; and third, the conclusion.
The passage from "Why is this? to "dwelling in the aspect of fear" is an exposition of the Dharma. The statement "all things do not exist" means that they are empty and non-existent;

this is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). "Practice" refers to the wisdom that takes emptiness as its object. If a Bodhisattva relies upon this wisdom of emptiness, they will have no fear.
As for the Arhat, because they rely on the Mahāyāna teaching yet dwell upon the aspects [of phenomena] while contemplating emptiness, they are so named.

"Abiding in the aspect of fear": this refers to the fact that the followers of the Two Vehicles have not yet cultivated the practice of the antidote to the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya*) outside of the Three Vehicles;
therefore, it is said they "have no practice. "Terror" refers to the death and rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*).

"Aspect" means that their wisdom abides in emptiness but does not understand names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*). "Abiding" refers to the benefit of these followers of the Two Vehicles. "Aspect" means that their own wisdom lacks understanding.
"Full. As for "abiding," other stages are termed "abidings. If one follows the Chinese convention, it should be called "the characteristic of abiding" (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*);

however, here we follow the Western [Indian] convention, thus it is named "abiding of the characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa-sthiti*). To say "as if a person were grasping a sword intending to come and harm oneself"—this is stated as an analogy.
Ignorance acting as craving is like the cause and effect; the armor is like the grasping. The transformation-death (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*) is like the sword. "The self" refers to the Arhat.
These followers of the Two Vehicles have already fulfilled the cultivation of their own stages, meaning they believe there is no birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).

However, because they now fall into the "subtle transformation birth-and-death" (*pariṇāmika-jarāmaraṇa*), it is called "harming oneself. This serves as an analogy for the perfected aspect. Therefore, it is said that the Arhat does not attain ultimate bliss.
The commentary states: This clarifies that since the Arhat is still subject to fear, one knows there is no ultimate bliss.

Because a person can serve as a place of refuge for the Tathāgata, they are called "one who does not seek refuge.

Regarding the five pairs of topics, the first four clarify the meaning of attainment and non-attainment, while the fifth provides a dual conclusion. Within the first four, there are two parts:

the first three clarify the distinction of the qualities of practice (*caryā-guṇa*), and the last one reveals the distinction of the qualities of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*). Within the qualities of practice, there are three sections.

First, breadth and narrowness; second, depth; third, coarseness and subtlety. Within these four [categories], the first clarifies what the Tathāgata has attained, while the latter clarifies what the two vehicles have not attained.

In each and every phrase, there are four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*): the first two clarify what the Tathāgata has attained, and the latter two clarify what the two vehicles have not attained—this being the reverse of the former two.
There is also an alternative interpretation, which clarifies the manifestation of the knowledge that "birth has been exhausted" and so forth.

Among the five pairs, the first four follow their respective order. First is the pair of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). There is no disparity in breadth between them.

As for the question, "Why is it that [the teaching] reaches only this as the Buddha’s skillful means? the commentary states: the followers of the Two Vehicles attain only the unconditioned, yet they speak of "no nirvāṇa."
The Tathāgata has fully realized and truly attained *nirvāṇa*. However, within the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), there are two kinds—namely, the true and the provisional;

this is the second pair. To say that only the Tathāgata [attains it] is the Buddha’s skillful means. The commentary states: This is the pair of the provisional and the real, also called the pair of the shallow and the deep.
The Tathāgata possesses both, and thus is said to "possess *nirvāṇa*. The Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) attain only the provisional, and thus are said to "lack it."

"Nirvāṇa. To say that only the Tathāgata attains it refers to the Buddha’s skillful means (*upāya*). The commentary states: Regarding the third pair, within the conventional analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), there are two types.

If a Śrāvaka attains only the conventional analytical cessation of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), whereas a Tathāgata fully realizes the conventional analytical cessation of both hindrances, one therefore says that the Tathāgata "attains nirvāṇa. This is the pair of the coarse and the subtle. To say "only" [the Tathāgata]...

"The Tathāgata has reached this Buddha-convenience. The commentary states: Within the provisional analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), there are two types, namely seeds (*bīja*) and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
If a Śrāvaka only severs the seeds and does not eliminate the habitual tendencies, whereas a Tathāgata completely severs both types, he is said to have attained *nirvāṇa*.
This refers to the opposition between seeds and habitual tendencies. It is said that only a Tathāgata attains *parinirvāṇa*, up to the point of reaching *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding the "elements" (*dhātu*): the commentary states that this refers to the contrast between the *dharmakāya* and liberation (*vimukti*). If it is that which is severed by the *śrāvakas*, it is merely termed the "body of liberation" (*vimuktikāya*).

If it is that attained by the Tathāgata, it is termed the "Dharma-body" (*dharmakāya*). As the Honored One of the three realms and the Lord of the four modes of birth, he is revered by humans and devas and upheld by the eight classes of beings;
therefore, it is said that the Tathāgata truly attains *nirvāṇa*. If the *śrāvakas* [attain it], it is merely a skillful means.
Furthermore, within the "Extensive Bodhi" (Vipula-bodhi), there are two sections. First, a general explanation that the śrāvakas do not attain the four types of wisdom; second, a specific exposition.

Regarding the statement from "Arhat" to "expounded as provisional meaning," the commentary states this is the general section. This has two parts. First, explaining how it was in the past... [The text continues with the description of the Tathāgata’s former deeds.]

The attainment of the four wisdoms is also the Mahāyāna. There are other sūtras which state that when followers of the two vehicles (dviyāna) observe and attain these four wisdoms, it is called "attaining a place of rest.
The above [explanation] was spoken according to the intentions of others; it is a teaching of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*), a skillful means for guidance, and not the true attainment.
Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is said to have attained it truly. Question: Why is the "transformed city" (*nirmāṇa-pura*) not considered an attainment?

In truth, it is taught expediently that there are two. Why are the sheep and deer not real? If so, why are three fully taught? The answer is: Nirvana is solely the fruit and virtue; it is provisionally and truly taught as two.
As for the accomplishment of tasks, there are distinctions between cause and effect and differences in their practice; thus, the three vehicles are taught.

Within the separate exposition, there are four sections: the four knowledges beginning with "the knowledge that birth has been exhausted. The text is divided into four parts, which constitute fourteen knowledges in total.

Regarding the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), these are further divided into four knowledges. As for the terms "knowledge of exhaustion" and "knowledge of non-arising":

when wisdom (*jñāna*) is able to sever delusions, it is called "exhaustion"; the wisdom attained within that state of exhaustion is termed "knowledge of exhaustion. This refers to knowing those afflictions...
The non-arising of future afflictions (*kleśa*) is called the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*). Within these two knowledges, they are distinguished into four types of knowledge.

That which takes as its object the exhaustion of birth and death is called "my births are exhausted. From within this, the knowledge that the holy life has been established (*brahmacarya-samāpanna-jñāna*) is further distinguished.

How is this known? It is because one cultivates the path of abandonment with the intention to sever birth and death; once birth and death are exhausted, the practice of the holy life is established. Therefore, it is called "exhaustion."
From within the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), the knowledge that "that which was to be done has been accomplished" (*kṛta-karaṇīya-jñāna*) is extracted.

Knowing that what is desirable will never again arise is called the knowledge that "there is no further existence" (*nāparaṃ itthattāya-jñāna*). Knowing that what is to arise will not arise because one no longer performs formative activities (*saṃskāra*) is called "that which was to be done has been accomplished. Therefore, it is known that from within the knowledge of non-arising, the knowledge that "that which was to be done has been accomplished" is extracted.

This is wisdom (*jñāna*). Furthermore, there are four objects of liberation: "My births have been exhausted; I shall not undergo further existence," which arises conditioned by the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*);

"The holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished," which arises conditioned by the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*); and within the knowledge of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), there are two types of arising insight.

First, the principles are briefly presented; second, the meaning of the "knowledge of non-exhaustion" (*ajñāta-jñāna*) is correctly elucidated. Within the former [section], there are two parts: first, the initial inquiry that raises the general inquiry;
second, the specific manifestation of its characteristics. "For what reason are there two kinds of death?"—this is the statement of the inquiry that initiates the question.

The term "intention" (*yi*) also carries three meanings. First, it is said that this serves as a general inquiry for the following four points: "For what reason are the four wisdoms of the two vehicles both not yet perfected?
According to the subsequent explanations, however, these are all individual inquiries; furthermore, in this context, they are not necessarily intended as a general summary. Second, [it is said]:...
Why is it that only the first person is questioned? Is the statement, "My births are not yet exhausted," a teaching of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*) by the Buddha?

Below, the specific explanation of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) has three parts: first, the question; second, the enumeration; and third, the explanation. Regarding the phrase, "What are the two?"—this is the question.
Regarding the phrase, "namely, death by fragmentation and inconceivable transformative death"—this is the enumeration. Regarding the phrase, "death by fragmentation"—this is the explanation.
Regarding the phrase "so-called false and deceptive sentient beings": the commentary states that this explains *paricchinna-bhava* (segmented existence).

Because [their] lifespan has a fixed limit according to the length determined by karma, each period of existence is distinct; thus it is called "segmented. Since a "segment" (*bhāga*) is a division (*vibhāga*), birth and death are themselves the segmented.

This is a *karmadhāraya* compound. As for being "false and deceptive," since they dwell within the three realms where both cause and effect are tainted (*sāsrava*), they are termed "false and deceptive. The word "not" [indicates...]
Regarding "inconceivable transformation leading to unsurpassed bodhi": the commentary states that its wondrous function is difficult to fathom, hence it is called "inconceivable" (*acintya*).
To alter the subsequent and transform the fundamental form is called "transformation" (*pariṇāma*). There are three types of attainment:

namely, the mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*) of Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas of great power, which persist until Nirvana, constantly receiving this body without interruption therein. Now...
To say that there is "arising" is incorrect. Since its essence (*tattva*) is not differentiated, how can one speak of arising? Now, the explanation is as follows:

the three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*) merely transform their original forms; they are not newly produced. Question: In this context, one intends to clarify that "my births have been exhausted.

Why, then, does it speak of two kinds of death? Answer: Here, according to the ultimate reality (*bhūta-artha*), the manifestation of signs is not death. This is because it is discussed in terms of the characteristic of impermanence (*anitya-lakṣaṇa*).

[The Buddha] proceeded. One should speak of both "birth" and "death"; however, because those who are born look upward [toward life], while those who die look with aversion [toward it], here we refer only to the two kinds of death based on that aversive contemplation.
Question: Since the three mentions of death clearly imply birth, why does he now clarify the three [stages] beginning with "the holy life has been established"?
Answer: In reality, he clarifies only that "my births have been exhausted. He did not intend to clarify the latter three [stages]. This is because he follows the momentum [of the teaching].
Because their meanings are interconnected, they are cited; in order to establish the first [of the four knowledges], they are explained collectively.

Second, the actual clarification that "my births have been exhausted. Within this, there are two parts: first, the clarification of the characteristics of the four knowledges; second, the conclusion that returns to the statement "my births have been exhausted.
Within the former, there are four [knowledges], which refer to the Four Truths. Regarding the phrase "among the two kinds of death, up to my births... [the text continues].

Regarding "that which has been exhausted": the commentary states that this clarifies being free from *pariccheda-jarā-maraṇa* (segmented birth and death), which is termed "birth having been exhausted.

It is not that *pariṇāmi-jarā-maraṇa* (transformative birth and death) does not exist; thus, it is called "not of definitive meaning" (*neyārtha*). Regarding the statement "the holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been established" because one has attained the realization of the fruit with remainder:

the commentary states this clarifies the wisdom of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*). Merely realizing the two bases of existence and non-existence is termed "the holy life has been established. "Brahma" (*brahma*) means purity; it is thus the Truth (*tattva*).
It remains as before. "Practice" refers to the cause. Regarding the statement, "From ordinary persons and devas up to those who have declared their task accomplished," the commentary states:
this clarifies the wisdom of the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*). Ordinary persons and devas merely suppress [afflictions] without severing them; they do not attain the wisdom of the path.

The seven [stages] consisting of the three fruits and four candidates (*phala-pratipannaka*) are able only to sever delusions, yet their tasks are not yet accomplished. Only the Arhat is able to eliminate false and deceptive afflictions.
"The exhaustion of afflictions is called 'having accomplished what was to be done. Regarding the statement that an Arhat 'will not undergo further existence,' the commentary says:
this clarifies the wisdom regarding the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*). Since the hindrance of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) has been severed, both the cause and its manifestation are absent;

thus, it is called 'not undergoing further existence. The above concludes the separate explanation of the four types of wisdom. Hereafter begins the second section, which summarizes [the preceding] by returning to the first wisdom, the wisdom regarding the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*)."

Regarding the statement, "It is not because one has exhausted all afflictions that one says 'there is no further existence,' but rather [because of the realization of the first fruit]," the commentary states:
Although the other three fruits were mentioned above, the intent was to clarify that for the first, "my births have already been exhausted."

Regarding the section on "having already established [the practitioner] within the conduct of Śakra and Brahmā," the text consists of two parts: first, a general statement clarifying that the obstacles have not been severed;
second, a detailed explanation of their distinctions. As for the passage from "Why is this? to "that which cannot be severed," the commentary states that this is the general summary.

Within this section, there is an error in the translation; it should not be accepted as is. It says that afflictions are not severed by the Two Vehicles because they pertain to all Three Vehicles; therefore, one should rather say that "there are obstacles."

It is not severed by the two vehicles (*dvaya-yāna*), for it does not obstruct them. Within the detailed exposition of the distinctions, there are two parts: first, the specific clarification of the four *vāsabhūmis*;
second, the clarification of the *avidyāvāsabhūmi*. Regarding the former, there are two sections: first, the presentation of the thesis, which has two sub-divisions;

second, the specific explanation of the two types [of *vāsabhūmis*]. Regarding the first of these, there are three parts: first, the indication of its form; second, the interrogation; third, the enumeration. As for the term "defilements" (*kleśa*)...
"There are two kinds. [Commentary: This states the number. "What are the two? [Commentary: This poses the question regarding the two.

"Namely, the afflictions of the underlying ground (*āśraya-kleśa*) and the arising afflictions (*utthāna-kleśa*). [Commentary: This enumerates their names. In the subsequent detailed explanation, there are two parts.
