An extensive analysis also contains four points, which correspond respectively as follows. Regarding the statement, "For what reason...
[it] can attain a defiled mind," the commentary states: this explains the first point. Regarding the phrase "momentary wholesome mind," it refers to the stainless *tathatā* (suchness).
This is because the nature of these two minds is not affliction (*kleśa*). Regarding the term "contact" (*sparśa*), it has the meaning of merging into a single flavor. This mind and the afflictions—

Since they are not unified into a single flavor, how can one speak of a defiled mind? "Mind" (*citta*) refers to the meaning of reality, namely *tathatā* (suchness). Regarding the statement, "The World-Honored One [said] up to 'defiled by the afflictions'": the commentary states that this explains the second point. Although its nature is pure, it is nevertheless defiled by the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vāsabhūmi*). Regarding the statement, "Self-nature is pure... difficult to comprehend": [this explains the third point]. It means that although the nature of the mind is pure, it is difficult to realize because it is obscured by adventitious defilements. Thus, it is said: "The self-nature of the mind is pure, yet it is difficult to comprehend. This is because, while the mind is originally pure, it is obscured by adventitious defilements; therefore, it is difficult to understand. Furthermore, regarding the statement, "The Tathāgata’s wisdom is subtle and profound": the commentary states that this explains the fourth point. [The commentary] states: This explains the third [point]. Since there are two names for the basis of the purity and defilement of sentient beings, it is indeed difficult to comprehend.

Regarding the statement "Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One... knows and sees according to reality," [the commentary] states: This explains the fourth [point] (within which there are ten explanations as set forth in the *Śūyāo*).
In the second section, the Tathāgata’s praise, there are two parts: first, internal rejoicing; second, verbal approval.
Regarding the statement that when Queen Śrīmālā reached the Buddha, he immediately rejoiced: this describes the first part, internal rejoicing.
Within the verbal approval, there are two [subsections], which are subsumed within the first four meanings; the first two [meanings] are not described here.

This is because their meaning is easy to understand. Regarding the statement "In this way and that way... it is also difficult to comprehend," the commentary says: the first part describes the preceding [point], while the third is not something that can be fathomed by an inferior intellect. Regarding the statement "These two dharmas... one can only believe the Buddha's words," the commentary says: [this refers to] the fact that these two dharmas are profound and subtle, and thus cannot be known through inference or logical reasoning. Therefore, one must rely solely on faith in the Buddha’s words. Furthermore, regarding the statement "The Tathāgata, having fully awakened to all phenomena," the commentary says: this means that the Tathāgata has realized all phenomena as they truly are, without error; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata. Regarding the statement "He teaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings," the commentary says: this means that the Tathāgata, out of great compassion, teaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings so that they may attain liberation. Regarding the statement "If one hears this Dharma and believes it," the commentary says: this means that if one hears this Dharma and develops faith, one will gradually attain liberation. Regarding the statement "If one does not believe it, one will fall into evil destinies," the commentary says: this means that if one does not believe this Dharma, one will instead fall into the three evil paths. Regarding the statement "Therefore, one should believe and accept it," the commentary says: this means that because of the aforementioned reasons, one should believe and accept it with utmost sincerity. Regarding the statement "One should not harbor doubt," the commentary says: this means that one should not entertain doubts or suspicions. The commentary states: The second section restates the preceding fourth point, that only a Buddha can know [this].
Within the chapter on the True Sons of the Tathāgata, there are three parts: first, the clear exposition of the benefits of faith; second, from the passage "After my parinirvāṇa... onwards.
This clarifies the praise of the benefits of faith. The section beginning with "Those who have faith in the Tathāgata" concludes the discussion on the benefits of faith.

Within the preceding portion, there are two parts: first, a brief explanation that those who possess faith can accord with the path and attain the ultimate; second, an extensive exposition of the five kinds of contemplation.
The passage from "If my disciples... up to "...attain the ultimate" is described as the first part: the brief explanation of faith. It says, "in accordance with faith."
This refers to the forty mental states (*citta*). "The increase of faith" refers to the four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
"Having relied upon clear faith" refers to attaining the four unshakable faiths (*aveṇikī śraddhā*) from the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward;

thus one is able to accord with the knowledge of the Dharma and attain the ultimate. The four unshakable faiths refer to the Three Jewels and the precepts. Regarding the extensive explanation of the five... [text ends].

Within the various types of contemplation, there are two parts: first, the explanation of the five contemplations; second, the summary. Within these five types of contemplation, there are two [sections]: the first two clarify the contemplation of defilement (*saṃkliṣṭa-vipaśyanā*);
the second has three kinds, clarifying the contemplation of purity (*viśuddha-vipaśyanā*). Within the former [contemplation of] defilement, there are two:

the first is the contemplation of the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), and the second is the contemplation of cause and effect. It says: "Following the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) up to the observation of karma."

The commentator states: The first contemplation concerns defilement (*saṃkleśa*). "Roots and mind" refers to the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*); "objects" refers to the six sense-fields (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*).
The body, which arises through causes and conditions, has no fixed nature; its conventional designations are likewise eternally without fixed reality. These are termed "mind" and "mental engagement."

"Speech and action" refers to the cause; "retribution" refers to the fruit. Regarding the statement, "observing the sleep of an Arhat who has attained the supreme, holy, and sovereign supernormal powers," the commentary states:
the second section clarifies the observation of purity. There are three observations, which are divided into two parts:
the first person clarifies the pure fruit, while the latter two distinguish the pure causes. The term "sleep" refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*); within the body of an Arhat, this sleep...
Once it is severed, one knows that this is the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*), because at this stage one looks up to and trains in it.

Furthermore, it is said that the entry into *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* by those of the two vehicles is similar to sleep; thus it is called "sleep. Regarding the statement "the bliss of mastery of mind and the bliss of dhyāna":

this means that having attained the bliss of the four dhyānas within the body, one constantly experiences the bliss of the four dhyānas within the body and always aspires to and delights in it. This is called the "mastery of the noble ones" (*āryavaśitā*).

"Penetration" refers to observing the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) attained by those of the three vehicles (*triyāna*). Regarding the statement, "The accomplishment of these five kinds of skillful means and observations," the commentary says:
this is the second summary. Regarding the statement, "From after my parinirvāṇa until entering the path of the Mahāyāna," [it refers to the period of practice].

The commentary states: The second [section] praises the benefits of faith. Because one possesses the superior knowledge that accords with the Dharma through faith, although one may be defiled by those [afflictions], one’s own nature remains pure; this is precisely the ultimate cause for entering the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the passage from "faith in the Tathāgata" to "not slandering the profound meaning," the commentary states: The third [section] concludes the benefits of faith.
In the "Chapter on the Lion’s Roar of Śrīmālā" within the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*, there are five sections: first, Śrīmālā requests and strives to speak;
second, the Tathāgata grants permission; third, Śrīmālā speaks correctly; fourth, having finished speaking, she bows her head at the Buddha's feet;

and fifth, the Tathāgata offers praise. Regarding the passage from "At that time, Śrīmālā... up to "...further spoke this meaning," the commentary states: the first is the request and striving to speak.

Regarding the statement "The Buddha spoke and immediately taught," the commentary says: this is the second point, the Tathāgata’s granting of permission, signifying that "now is precisely the right time.
Regarding the third point, the actual teaching itself, there are two parts: first, excluding those who are virtuous as they are not the ones to be converted;

second, from the passage beginning "all the multitudes" onwards, focusing specifically on the wicked to clarify the benefit of conversion. Within the first of these two parts, there are again two sub-sections: first, citing three types of virtuous people.

Regarding "persons," the two vows and these various [categories] below have already been excluded in general. Within the preceding section, there are again two parts: first, a brief explanation; second, a detailed explanation beginning with "What are... and so forth.
As for the passage from "Śrīmālā said to the Buddha" up to "entering the path of the Mahāyāna," the commentary states that this is the brief explanation.
Śrīmālā says: "There are three kinds of good persons who do not require conversion; that is to say, those who do not give rise to slander regarding the profound meaning."
"Slandering" means to distance oneself from and cause injury to [the teaching]. It is able to give rise to roots of goodness and produce great merit;
furthermore, it enables one to seek unsurpassed enlightenment, which is called "entering the path of the Mahāyāna. Within the extensive explanation, there are two parts:

first, the inquiry; second, the exposition. Regarding the phrase "What are the three?": the commentary states that this is an inquiry. Since it has already been stated that there are three kinds of virtuous persons, what are they? In...
The commentary consists of three parts, which are divided into three sections corresponding to the enumeration of three types of names. The first concerns self-benefit; the second, benefiting others;

and the third, the reverent acknowledgment that the profound meaning is beyond one's own sphere and belongs to the Tathāgata. Regarding the passage from "If a son of good family" to "one who possesses wisdom regarding the profound Dharma," the commentary states:
the first [section] concerns self-benefit. Within the reality of things as they are (*yathārtha*), one does not give rise to slander.

To be free from self-destruction is called self-benefit. Regarding the statement, "If a son of good family... up to... one who accords with the knowledge of the Dharma," the commentary states: this is the second [point], benefiting others.
Being able to accord with the knowledge of the Dharma and extensively benefit sentient beings is called benefiting others.

Regarding the statement, "If a son of good family... up to... looking up to and relying upon the Tathāgata," the commentary states: this is the third [point], looking up to and relying upon the Buddha. This is...
Regarding the phrase "having set aside these sons and daughters of good family," because it pertains to the wisdom of abiding (*sthiti-bhāga-jñāna*), it is described as the second conclusion.
Regarding the phrase "all other sentient beings... until they have been tamed," it is described as the second point concerning those who are unwholesome.

This clarifies the transformative guidance. Regarding the statement, "At that time, he went to the Buddha’s feet," the commentary says: this is the fourth [section], paying homage at the Buddha’s feet with his head.
Regarding the statement, "The Buddha said, 'Excellent, excellent! You are able to explain this meaning,'" the commentary says:

this is the fifth [section], the Tathāgata’s praise and commendation. Within the third [section], the section on relying on practice, there are three parts: first, the Tathāgata and others return; second, "At that time... [and so forth].
At that time, the World-Honored One entered the Jeta Grove and reiterated his teaching. Three times Śakra, Lord of Devas, arrived and joyfully practiced it;
the great assembly likewise practiced it. Within the section on his return, there are two parts: first, the Tathāgata’s return to the kingdom; second, his entry into the city.
Regarding the latter, Queen Śrīmālā enters the city. Within the Tathāgata’s return, there are two parts: first, the World-Honored One’s return to the kingdom; second, at that time, Queen Śrīmālā.
[The text] below states: "At that time, the World-Honored One returned to the kingdom of Śrāvastī. The commentary says:
This is the first instance of the Tathāgata returning to his native land. Regarding "seven *tāla* trees": one tree is seven *ren* high; one *ren* is seven feet high.
Thus, one tree is forty-nine feet high. Seven trees amount to three hundred and forty-three feet. It is said that [this distance] was superior in time.

Regarding the passage "Śrīmālā arrives and fully recollects the Buddha," the commentary states: This refers to the second queen, Śrīmālā, who follows her recollection of the Tathāgata’s three types of activity (trikarma).
Regarding the passage "she returns to the city and all turn toward the Mahāyāna," the commentary states: This describes the second [event], Śrīmālā’s entry into the city.
Although the queen resides in the palace, which is distinct from the royal city, she is said to "enter the city" here. Within this restatement, there are three parts; first—
The Tathāgata addressed Śakra. Second, as soon as he was thought of, he arrived. Third, the Buddha preached for him to clarify the entrustment.
Regarding the statement, "At that time, the World-Honored One [addressed] up to Śakra, the Lord of Devas," the commentary says: this describes the first instance, the addressing of Śakra.

Regarding the statement, "He arrived at that moment and stood before the Buddha," the commentary says: this describes the second instance, arriving immediately upon being thought of. Regarding the third point, the Buddha preached for him.
Within the section on the entrustment (*parindanā*), there are two parts: first, the Tathāgata’s preaching of the sūtra; second, the actual explanation of the entrustment.
Regarding the passage from "At that time, the World-Honored One" up to "extensively preached this sūtra," the commentary states: this is the first part, the preaching of the sūtra.
Within the second entrustment, there are two parts. The first is the general entrustment to Śakra and Ānanda; the second, from "Furthermore, Kauśika" onwards, is the specific entrustment to Śakra.
Within the general part, there are two sections. The first encourages upholding through the difficulty of the benefit;

the second, from "Then Śakra Devendra addressed the Buddha," onwards, concerns the inquiry into practice. Within the former [the encouragement], there are two: first, the address to Śakra; second, [the subsequent section].
Again, he addressed Ānanda: "The preceding section has three parts: first, a general address and exhortation to uphold [the teaching]; second, a comparative evaluation of its superiority;

and third, from 'Therefore' onwards, a summary of the reception and upholding. Regarding the statement, "Having spoken thus, [he] arrived at this sutra," the commentary says: "This is the first part, the general address."

Within the section on comparative evaluation, there are two parts: first, the exaltation of other practices as being vastly superior; second, the demonstration that even those [other practices] cannot compare to upholding this sutra.

Regarding the passage from "Kauśika" to "pāramitā," the commentary states: this is the first instance of exalting its superiority. Regarding the passage from "If, moreover... to "explains it to others," the commentary states:

this is the second instance, wherein it is shown that [other practices] fall short by comparison. Regarding the passage from "For this reason... to "analyzes and explains in detail," the commentary states: [this concludes the section].
The commentary states that this is a summary. Regarding the passage from "Again he addressed Ānanda" up to "extensively explained to the fourfold assembly," the commentary states:
this is the second address to Ānanda. Within the second inquiry concerning the upholding of the sūtra, there are two parts: first, the inquiry of Śakra, Lord of Devas, regarding its upholding;

second, the Tathāgata’s formal response. Regarding the passage from "At that time, Śakra, Lord of Devas... up to "...how should it be upheld? the commentary states: this is the inquiry into the name of the sūtra.

Please uphold this Dharma. Within the Tathāgata’s correct response, there are two parts. First, praising the profundity and subtlety of the Dharma as being like seeing that which is utterly transcendent;
second, the present section below. The former was briefly explained previously. Within that [first part], there are two sections: first, extolling that the sutra is not the realm of the Two Vehicles;
second, extolling the subtlety and wonder of the sutra. Regarding the passage from "The Buddha said" to "knowing and seeing," the commentary states: this extols its being beyond [their] sphere.
Regarding the statement "Kauśika, up to the mass of great merit," the commentary says this is an exclamation praising the sublime.

Within the discourse delivered by the Tathāgata, there are three parts: first, the Tathāgata’s command to listen; second, Śakra and the others receiving the instruction; and third, the actual delivery of the discourse.

Regarding the phrase "Now you should attend to it with mindfulness," the commentary says this is the first part, the command permitting the discourse. Regarding the phrase "At that time, Śakra... up to "received [the teaching]," [the commentary continues as follows].

The Teacher explains: The second part clarifies the reception [of the teaching]. Regarding the statement, "As the Buddha said, up to 'thus should it be upheld' by the Lion’s Roar," the commentary states:

The third part is the formal exposition and formal response. Within this response, there are two sections: the first phrase answers the previous question regarding the name, and the subsequent phrase answers the previous question regarding the upholding.
Within the specific entrustment to Śakra, there are three parts: first, praising the profundity of the sūtra; second, the formal entrustment; and third...
"Receiving the Honored One’s instruction": from "Furthermore... up to "...entering the path of the one or two vehicles," the commentary states this is the praise of its profundity. "Kauśika...
up to "...extensively explaining and distinguishing," the commentary states this is the second section, the formal entrustment. "Śakra...

up to "...receiving the Honored One’s instruction upon his head," the commentary states this is the third section, the compliance with the teaching. "Then the Lord of Devas... up to "...praising those who practice it," the commentary states...
It is said: This is the third section on the classification of practice. Within it, the true and the cursive styles have not yet established fixed rules.

If there are those who transcribe [this], they should apply their minds and efforts with diligence, looking up to the venerable Master for inspiration throughout the year. From beginning to end, they must never abandon this for even a moment.
At the Bao-guo Monastery in the Jiè region, starting from the beginning of spring, he was ordered to lecture on the Śrīmālā-sūtra and the [Vimśatikā-]... [Twenty Verses].
Treatise: Following what was gathered and excerpted, and having consulted on what had not yet been heard, once I had received these instructions, I compiled them into this *Shuji* (Commentary).
However, as the text is concise while the meaning is vast, it is somewhat difficult to peruse.

Furthermore, in the second year of the Yifeng era, at Tayuan Temple in the eastern capital of Luoyang, I reconstructed and expanded upon it, elaborating the phrasing and unfolding the meaning to remedy omissions and deficiencies. I have extensively cited scriptural evidence, hoping that future students will [benefit from it].
Do not [be negligent] regarding this. This is a record commissioned by Yi.
